figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: The Evolving Agent Teams framework. Team execution runs coding agents on the task through tool use and execution feedback. Team evolution acts as a meta-optimizer: it analyzes the past success and failure patterns, and adapts the team composition, role specialization, coordination protocol, and knowledge management for the current stage of discovery.

citing_sentences: It operates at two levels, following the loop shown in Figure 2: at the team evolution level, a supervisor agent monitors each team’s execution, analyzes success and failure patterns, and designs the next team $T_{v+1}$.

abstract: The rapid progress of software engineering agents drives interest in applying them to open-ended problems such as GPU kernel optimization. However, we find that existing coding agents converge to local optima on real-world, expert-written kernels (e.g., FlashInfer). We introduce Evolving Agent Teams, a multi-agent framework that escapes such local optima. It features (1) a central supervisor that diagnoses each local optimum and restructures a team of agents; and (2) a persistent file system that comprises a learning document, an evolution history, and per-team artifacts, grounding restructuring with accumulated experience. Under a matched token budget, Evolving Agent Teams consistently outperforms strong coding-agent baselines. With an extended token budget, Evolving Agent Teams generates a CUDA kernel that reaches $1.2\times$ mean speedup over the production FlashInfer MLA paged decode kernel from scratch and wins on 36 of 47 production workloads from FlashInfer-Bench ($0.86$–$0.99\times$ on the remaining 11). It also demonstrates superior performance on tasks such as KDA prefill on AMD MI350X ($3.01\times$ over vLLM) and NVIDIA B200 ($3.44\times$ over FlashKDA), MoE expert-offload serving on Apple silicon ($30.3$ tokens/s decode for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in MLX 4-bit on a 48 GB M4 Pro), and RoboDojo robot manipulation ($62.1$ on held-out seeds vs. $55.3$ for the best leaderboard entry). Code is available at https://github.com/caoshiyi/EAT.

sections.body: The paper argues that coding agents make fast early progress on GPU kernels but converge to local optima well below expert baselines. Codex 5.5 xHigh reaches only 28% of expert performance on the MLA decode kernel with a USD 1K budget, and a fixed four-role team built with Claude Code reaches only 55%. The proposed Evolving Agent Teams framework changes team organization during the run and explores over 100 team configurations on MLA decode. Under a matched token budget, Claude Code plateaus at 0.51× the FlashInfer kernel, while the framework reaches 0.74×. With an extended budget it reaches 1.21× mean speedup, faster on 36 of 47 workloads, against 0.61× for the previous best result from K-Search.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing coding agents stall at local optima on expert-written GPU kernels, so the paper evolves the agent team during optimization.

sections.body: The section groups prior work into three areas. Multi-agent systems such as ChatDev, MetaGPT, DyLAN, and AgentVerse use fixed roles or regenerate the group, and the paper says its framework operates over multi-day horizons and keeps a persistent global file system across restructurings. Self-improving and evolutionary methods, including Reflexion, Voyager, FunSearch, OpenEvolve, AlphaEvolve, and ADAS, either improve one agent within a fixed role or use population-based search with LLM-driven mutation. This work uses no population. Meta-optimization work such as Meta-Harness optimizes the surrounding harness, whereas this work adapts the search process itself. K-Search uses a fixed two-role configuration.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work mostly fixes agent roles or uses population search; this work restructures one team under a persistent supervisor.

sections.body: The paper defines an agent team as a configuration of roles, coordination, and knowledge management, and treats existing systems as fixed on all three. In Evolving Agent Teams, a supervisor agent runs when a team finishes or on a fixed-interval cron job. It checks progress, reflects on failure patterns such as drifting to easy paths or stalling in debugging, and designs the next team. Roles are invented rather than selected from a predefined set; examples include a Profiling Scientist, a Challenger, a Primitive Study Agent, and a Knowledge Integrator. Each team agent has shell access. A persistent file system holds a learnings document, per-team artifacts, and an evolution history, so each team inherits prior work. The section reports no quantitative results.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: A supervisor diagnoses each plateau, rewrites roles, coordination, and knowledge management, with a persistent file system carrying experience across teams.

sections.body: The evaluation covers four kernel tasks: FA4 on B200 with 24 workloads, GDN prefill on B200 with 100, MLA paged decode on H100 with 47, and fused GEMM+AllReduce on H100 with 5. Speedup is the geometric mean of baseline over kernel latency, so values below 1.0× are slower than the baseline. Baselines are Claude Code with Opus 4.6, a fixed four-role team, Codex, K-Search, and CUDAForge. Each main setting runs twice and the better result is reported, while the ablation runs are single runs. Under the budget-controlled setting, the evolving team reaches 0.75× on MLA, against a Claude Code plateau of 0.44–0.51×. With extra budget, GDN prefill reaches 4.06× and G+AR reaches 1.49× overall. The authors state that two runs limit statistical conclusions.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: At matched budget the evolving team beats Claude Code on the four tasks, and reaches 1.21× on MLA decode with extra budget.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the main claim: strong coding agents converge to local optima on GPU kernels, and a supervisor that restructures the team, grounded in a persistent file system, helps escape them. The method outperforms coding-agent baselines under a matched token budget on four kernel tasks and, with more budget, surpasses the FlashInfer MLA decode kernel at 1.21× mean speedup across 47 workloads. The section also cites strong results on KDA prefill, MoE expert offload on Apple silicon, and robot manipulation. The stated limitation is that each main setting runs twice and the Section 4.7 settings run once, which limits statistical comparisons. A cost-versus-performance Pareto analysis and a controlled study of noisier domains are left as future work.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Evolving teams surpass FlashInfer MLA decode at 1.21× mean speedup; two runs per main setting limit statistical comparisons.

sections.body: This work was done at the Sky Computing Lab. The authors thank SemiAnalysis, Amazon, AMD, and NVIDIA for compute support. Shiyi Cao and Dacheng Li are supported by the Amazon Fellowship. The section makes no claims about results and reports no experimental evidence; it lists funding and support only.

sections.body: Appendix A (Table 3) lists roles the supervisor invented, grouped into implementation, analysis, knowledge, quality assurance, and architecture; examples include Workload Analyst, Challenger, and Dead-End Revisitor. Appendix B is a case study showing that the fixed four-role team starts slowly on MLA decode because a shared-memory layout bug is split across agents, which the authors attribute to team structure rather than capability. Appendix C gives single-run details for KDA prefill on MI350X at 3.01×, on B200 at 3.44×, and on B300 at 3.54×, plus MoE offload on Apple silicon and RoboDojo at 62.1 on held-out seeds. Appendix D reports matched-budget solo ablations on MI350X and on MoE offload, with Table 4 giving the offload results.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists supervisor-invented roles, a slow-start case study, extra settings, and matched-budget solo ablations.
